summary: Specifies how Bidirectional Forwarding Detection for multipoint networks can give sub-second failover for routers running PIM Sparse Mode. It defines an extension to the PIM Hello message used to start a point-to-multipoint BFD session.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers quickly check that their neighbors are still there, so multicast traffic takes another path almost right away.

questions: how fast does pim-sm failover with bfd
subtitle: Using multipoint BFD so PIM-SM routers notice a failed neighbor in under a second instead of 105 seconds.

tldr.problem: When a PIM-SM router such as the Designated Router fails, neighbors by default take 105 seconds to notice, which hurts multicast service.
tldr.mechanism: A router advertises a new BFD Discriminator option (type 39) in its PIM Hello. Neighbors then join a point-to-multipoint BFD session with that router and treat a BFD failure as the neighbor being gone.
tldr.outcome: Failure detection becomes sub-second, while PIM and BFD themselves are not changed. If the option disappears, neighbors fall back to normal PIM-SM behavior.

today: RFC 9186 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2022, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PIM-SM Needs Faster Failure Detection
sections.content:
Faster control plane convergence reduces traffic loss caused by stale routing information and transient loops. In PIM-SM, one router on each shared segment (such as Ethernet) is elected as the Designated Router (DR) and acts for the directly connected hosts. If the DR fails, multicast service for those hosts suffers, because the default failure detection interval for PIM-SM routers is 105 seconds.

Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) was first defined for point-to-point paths. RFC 8562 extends BFD to multipoint and multicast networks, which matches PIM-SM on a LAN segment. In such a point-to-multipoint (P2MP) session the monitored router is the head and the other routers are tails. Using BFD Demand mode creates less BFD state than Asynchronous mode. This RFC defines monitoring of a PIM-SM router with P2MP BFD and a PIM extension to bootstrap the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally routers wait a very long time, 105 seconds, before they admit a neighbor is gone. That is like waiting almost two minutes before noticing your friend left the room.

sections.title: The BFD Discriminator PIM Hello Option
sections.content:
The new optional PIM Hello option tells neighbors which BFD session to join. It has three fields: OptionType (39), OptionLength (MUST be 4) and HeadDiscriminator, a 4-octet field that MUST be included, MUST NOT be zero and equals the My Discriminator value the head allocated for its BFD session.

If OptionLength is not 4, the option is malformed and the receiver MUST stop processing PIM Hello options. If the discriminator is zero, the option is invalid and the receiver MUST ignore it. In both cases the receiver SHOULD log a notification, under the control of a throttling logging mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small note in the router's regular greeting that says 'listen for my heartbeat, my code number is this'. A code number of zero is not allowed.

sections.title: Monitoring a PIM Router with Multipoint BFD
sections.content:
The head MUST create a BFD session of type MultipointHead and MUST include the BFD Discriminator option in its PIM Hellos. Any PIM-SM router, whatever its role, MAY become a head, but operators should choose heads carefully to control the volume of BFD Control traffic on the segment. A router that monitors the head is a tail. When a tail sees the option in a Hello, it MAY create a MultipointTail session.

For the tail to demultiplex correctly, the source address and My Discriminator of the BFD packets MUST match the source address and HeadDiscriminator of the PIM Hello. If they do not, the tail cannot monitor the head, though regular PIM-SM mechanisms stay fully operational.

If the tail detects a MultipointHead failure, it MUST delete the corresponding neighbor state and follow the RFC 7761 procedures for the DR and for neighbor state deletion after the neighbor timeout expires. If the head stops serving the function that prompted monitoring, it MUST stop including the option and SHOULD shut down the BFD session following RFC 8562. When the option disappears, the tail SHOULD close its MultipointTail session without affecting PIM state, reverting to RFC 7761 procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The watched router keeps sending quick heartbeats. Its neighbors listen, and if the heartbeat stops they immediately treat it as gone instead of waiting a long time.

sections.title: DR Load Balancing and BFD Encapsulation
sections.content:
With PIM Designated Router Load Balancing (RFC 8775), any router advertising the DRLB-Cap option can become a head. It sets the session state to Up only if it is a Group Designated Router (GDR) Candidate. For each GDR Candidate that includes the BFD Discriminator option, the PIM DR MUST create a MultipointTail session, demultiplexing by My Discriminator and source IP address. If the DR detects a failure, it MUST remove that router from the GDR Candidate list and immediately send a new DRLB-List option.

When the head sends BFD Control packets, it MUST set the TTL or Hop Limit to 255, and received packets for the session MUST be discarded if the TTL or Hop Limit is not 255. It MUST use the group address ALL-PIM-ROUTERS as the destination, which is 224.0.0.13 for IPv4 and ff02::d for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: If several helpers share the work, the boss drops any helper whose heartbeat stops and tells the others at once. Heartbeats only count if they come from right next door.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has allocated OptionType value 39, length 4, named BFD Discriminator Option, in the PIM-Hello Options registry.

The document only accelerates detection of a failure that affects PIM functionality, and the operation of either protocol is not changed. The security considerations of RFC 5880, RFC 5881, RFC 7761, RFC 8562 and RFC 8775 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: This only makes routers notice problems faster. It does not change how either protocol works, so the same safety rules still apply.
